captions.text: Picture a northern village, on a night of high wind: electricity is worth next to nothing.
In a yard, a big dark silo is waiting.
They call it a sand battery…
and yet the largest one in service, in Finland, has no sand in it!
It holds about two thousand tonnes of crushed soapstone, and it gives back heat, not electricity.
Let’s follow one single grain of that stone.
It doesn’t move: the heat comes to find it.
Under the roof, it starts with the air: a blower drives it through resistors.
The current makes it very hot.
Here is our grain, in the dark, right up against a stainless pipe.
It warms, very slowly, and hands its heat on to its neighbour.
And the stone waits, at a mean of about four hundred degrees.
Then the wind drops, and electricity turns dear again.
A second blower draws the air back through the stone, and the exchanger gives its heat to the water.
The hot water runs underground to the village, and at the school, a radiator warms up.
That is the whole story: a gust of wind, a grain of stone, a lot of patience…
and a warm classroom.
Which leaves the real question: how much does this silo give back?
When full, it holds two hundred and seventeen megawatt-hours above the ambient air.
Sixty-nine come out at one megawatt.
A hundred and five come out afterwards, at falling power.
And forty-three stay in the stone, too cold for the network.
A capacity only means something at a given power!
The maker quotes up to a hundred megawatt-hours, without saying at what power.
Our model finds sixty-nine at one megawatt: the gap comes down to the size of a blower,
which nobody publishes.
A few landmarks: four views, the village, the silo, one pipe in the stone and the equipment floor.
Click any part: its sheet opens, and you can listen to its story.
One guide tells of the building site, another of how the silo joins its village.
The simulation lets you change everything.
Six lessons, with quizzes, explain the physics.
Ten sheets gather the drawings.
One last thing: this lab is an educational reconstruction, independent and generic.
It is neither an official plan nor a maker’s product, and this village exists nowhere.
Pipes, insulation, blowers, where the machines stand: none of it is published,
all of it is our reading or calculation.
Unless I quote a source, the figures come from our simulation.
And we have found no independent measurement of these machines.
Over to you!

segments.title: The village: from cheap current to the school

captions.text: Welcome to the village, at the forest’s edge: the whole story runs along its road.
Far off, the wind turbines set the price, without one cable to the silo.
The line brings the current, when it costs next to nothing.
Transformer and annex await it at the silo’s foot.
The silo itself shows nothing of what it hides.
Two pipes come down along its wall.
The water runs along a trench, drawn open for you, as far as the school and the houses of the village.
And the old boiler plant stands by, as a backup.
One precaution: a silo like this one is an industrial installation, subject to the rules of each country.
Here is the machine, a quarter open, like a cake someone has already started.
At the bottom, the slab, then an insulation that has to carry it all.
Above them, six metres of stone, and all its pipes.
Around it, insulation and cladding fit into half a metre.
Right at the top, the equipment floor, under its conical roof.
These colours come from the simulation,
and they are false colour: stone at four hundred degrees does not glow.
Let’s open half the silo.
The core is hotter than the edge, and yet nothing stirs in the stone.
Let’s pull the layers apart, from the slab to the roof.
Six metres of stone in thirteen metres of silo: all the rest protects it, or serves it.
Let’s zoom in.
Here is a block of stone, with our grain somewhere inside it.
A pipe goes down, turns round in its bend at the bottom, and climbs back.
At the top, a loop lets the pipe grow, and a header joins it to its neighbours.
Two blocks, two zones: the core and the edge.
And on the table, two samples, magnified for you.
In section, the heat spreads around the pipe, in rings.
The maker says a metre of sand heated on one side takes over eight days to reach a hundred degrees on the other.
Our simulation finds seven point four days.
Heat crawls: so it is fetched with a pipe about every fifty centimetres.

segments.title: Where the current and the heat go
